content: Umbilical hernia is a congenital defect that is particularly common in infants of African descent, although it can also be acquired later in life. The first documented case of an umbilical hernia with rupture was published by Dr. Henry Porter in 1855, and the first surgical case was reported by Dr. M.G. Oxley in 1876. The pathophysiology of umbilical hernia involves a weakness or incomplete formation of the abdominal fascia, which can result in herniation in newborns. During the fifth to tenth weeks of gestation, the intestines grow rapidly and temporarily protrude outside the abdominal cavity. Normally, this is followed by re-entry into the abdominal cavity and narrowing of the umbilical ring, completing the formation of the abdominal wall. Failure in this process can lead to an umbilical hernia. Umbilical hernias can be caused by congenital malformation of the navel or acquired due to increased intra-abdominal pressure from factors such as obesity, heavy lifting, chronic coughing, or multiple pregnancies. It is important to differentiate umbilical hernias from other types of hernias, such as epigastric, Spigelian, or incisional hernias. In the United States, umbilical hernias affect approximately 23 per 100,000 newborns and occur equally in males and females. Common risk factors include infancy, pregnancy, African American ethnicity, mucopolysaccharide storage diseases, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and Down syndrome. Most umbilical hernias are asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously, typically by the age of two years. However, complications such as incarceration, strangulation, skin discoloration, and ascites can occur. Clinically, umbilical hernias present as a soft swelling over the belly button that becomes more prominent when the infant sits up, cries, or strains. The bulge may flatten when the infant is lying on their back and calm. The size of the hernia can range from less than 1 cm to over 5 cm. Treatment depends on the size of the defect, the patient’s age, and cosmetic considerations. Most defects close spontaneously by the age of two. Families should be counseled about signs of complications, such as abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and a tender, hard mass at the umbilicus, which may indicate incarceration. Physical examination typically reveals a protruding umbilical mass, which should be assessed in both standing and supine positions, with or without the Valsalva maneuver, to determine the size of the hernia. There are no specific laboratory or ultrasound findings associated with uncomplicated umbilical hernias. However, ultrasound may be useful in diagnosing complications such as incarceration or strangulation. Surgical intervention is indicated for hernias larger than 2 cm, those with an elephant’s trunk appearance, hernias that do not close spontaneously by the age of 5 to 6 years, symptomatic hernias, or those that increase in size after the age of 1 to 2 years. Surgery for uncomplicated umbilical hernias is performed under general anesthesia as an outpatient procedure. Mesh implantation may be used to bridge the defect or as a preperitoneal mesh with suture repair. Postoperative recovery is typically uneventful, but recurrence can occur in patients with elevated intra-abdominal pressures. Laparoscopic techniques are reserved for large or recurrent hernias. There are no established measures for the primary prevention of umbilical hernias. Management often involves watchful waiting and educating parents about the natural course of the condition, as most hernias resolve within the first few years of life. In cases of incarceration, treatment includes intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression, and emergent surgery.
